summary.text: Ocean heat content is the energy that the oceans absorb and store, and it is an important sign of global warming.
It is worked out by measuring ocean temperature at many places and depths, then adding up the change in energy over an ocean basin or the whole ocean.
Its steady rise from 1971 to 2018 made up over 90% of Earth's excess energy from global warming, driven mainly by human greenhouse gas emissions.

paragraphs.heading: What it measures
paragraphs.text: Ocean heat content is the amount of energy that the world's oceans take in and hold. Scientists track it as one of the key signs of global warming. It is never given as a single absolute figure. Instead it is reported as a change from a chosen baseline, called an anomaly, and positive values show how much heat the ocean has taken up.

paragraphs.heading: Why the ocean matters for climate
paragraphs.text: The oceans are central to keeping Earth's climate steady. Water in the sea has a high heat capacity, meaning it can soak up huge amounts of energy while its temperature barely moves. Oceans also spread across 70% of the planet's surface. Keeping track of ocean heat, and of how it shifts over the years, is key to understanding climate and to building models of it.

paragraphs.heading: Ships and robot floats
paragraphs.text: Since before 1960, research ships and fixed stations around the world have measured the temperature of the sea at its surface and further down. Since 2000 they have been joined by Argo, a growing fleet of nearly 4000 robot floats. These floats record temperature anomalies, which reveal how ocean heat content is changing.

paragraphs.heading: Where the extra heat goes
paragraphs.text: From 1971 to 2018, ocean heat content rose steadily, and that rise made up more than 90% of the extra energy Earth gained from global warming. Scientists put the warming trend for 1961–2022 at 0.43 ± 0.08 W/m², speeding up by roughly 0.15 ± 0.04 W/m² each decade. By 2020, around a third of the added energy had reached below 700 meters. The five highest readings for the top 2000 meters all came between 2020 and 2024. Greenhouse gas emissions from human activity are the main cause of this rise.

paragraphs.heading: Uneven warming
paragraphs.text: The top 2000 meters of the ocean have warmed on average since the 1970s, but not at the same pace everywhere. The subpolar North Atlantic has warmed more slowly. The Southern Ocean, by contrast, has taken in an outsized share of the heat. It also shows the biggest warming in the deep water below 2000 meters when set against the other basins.

paragraphs.heading: Effects on life and coasts
paragraphs.text: Changing ocean temperatures have large effects on living systems, both at sea and on land. Coastal ecosystems, and the people who depend on what those ecosystems provide, feel several of these impacts. Direct effects include shifts in sea level and sea ice, changes in how intense the water cycle is, and sea creatures moving to new waters.
